disease_info: Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features is characterized by a full major depressive episode accompanied by delusions and/or hallucinations that are present only during the mood episode. The psychotic content is often mood-congruent (e.g., themes of guilt, worthlessness, or deserved punishment) and can significantly worsen impairment and risk, including suicidality. The course may be single-episode or recurrent, frequently associated with severe functional decline in work, self-care, and relationships, and it often presents subacutely rather than as a sudden break. It is distinguished from primary psychotic disorders by the absence of psychosis outside depressive episodes and from bipolar disorder by the lack of manic or hypomanic episodes.

narrative.stressor: About nine months ago, Karen took on a lead role in a complex audit engagement while simultaneously ramping up preparation for her CPA exams, stacking late nights at the firm on top of early-morning study sessions. Her usual perfectionism around spreadsheets and reports intensified as deadlines approached, and she began turning down hikes, photography trips, and social plans to "catch up" on work she already knew was technically complete. Over the next several months, colleagues and her spouse noticed she was increasingly withdrawn and preoccupied with the idea that any minor error in her work would ruin her career, yet she resisted cutting back on responsibilities or taking time off. When she started insisting that certain clients were secretly auditing her every move and became too distressed to finalize basic reports, her manager and husband persuaded her to see a psychiatrist after she broke down in a meeting and admitted she could no longer trust her own judgment.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m convinced I’ve made some terrible mistake in the books and that people are secretly watching everything I do, even though everyone keeps telling me it’s fine.”

narrative.stressor: Peter’s difficulties began after a back injury on a volunteer fire call led to chronic pain and ultimately forced him to stop most handyman work about a year ago, sharply cutting the household income. At first he tried to fill his time with gardening, soccer, and home-brewing, but as medical bills accumulated and he worried about his wife carrying the financial load, he gradually withdrew from league games and community events, spending more time alone in the garage and avoiding conversations about money. Over seven months, his preoccupation with unpaid bills and the possibility of losing their home deepened to the point that he stopped opening mail and insisted that the bank and utility companies were sending him hidden messages of blame and judgment. His wife finally convinced him to seek psychiatric help after he refused to attend their book club because he was sure neighbors were "in on" a plan to expose him as a failure and he admitted he was terrified to answer the phone or leave the house.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep hearing the bank and bill collectors talking about me, like they’re sending me messages that I’ve ruined everything, even when no one else hears anything.”

narrative.stressor: Barbara’s downturn began after her mother, who had been her closest companion and co-planner of church socials and county fair booths, died unexpectedly about ten months ago. At first she threw herself into organizing the funeral luncheon and community events, but as the seasons changed and familiar traditions arrived without her mother, she found it harder to attend gatherings, leaving others to run the coffee stand and skipping her usual theater rehearsals. Over the following seven months, neighbors noticed she was no longer tending her garden or showing up for walks along the Fox River, and she admitted to a close friend that evenings in her quiet house felt unbearable and that she felt like all the joy had been drained out of the town. When she stopped baking for potlucks, stayed in bed most mornings, and tearfully told her pastor that she couldn’t see any point in getting up because nothing in her life felt enjoyable anymore, he encouraged her and her sister to seek a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I don’t enjoy anything I used to love—church socials, baking, even talking with neighbors all feel empty now.”
